A guide to Lacanian concepts: from original texts to personal practice

When encountering “the Other,” “retroaction,” “the divided subject,” “full speech,” “half-saying,” or “sinthome,” the difficulty often lies beyond defining an individual word: why do these concepts appear in the same account, and how do they connect to personal models, writing, and tools? This guide approaches them through those relations, for first reading and later review. It offers conceptual explanation alongside the main reading route. Begin wherever a difficulty arises, then return to the original essay.

One important line of inquiry Lacan offers this site is: how do people express themselves through language and images received from others, and how do expression and its return reveal that they do not fully coincide with that account? Later expression can change the meaning of earlier speech; an established self-image can also be challenged by new encounters. The later discussions of knots and the sinthome further ask how these different relations connect in a person's concrete existence. Bringing them into model collaboration and engineering realization is work this site develops further.

First identify the level you are reading

Reading level What it does What to attend to
Lacan's account Develops concepts of the subject, language, identification, desire, and the three registers within psychoanalytic questions The period, question, and conceptual relations of the source text.
This site's philosophical development Uses these concepts to understand expression, oneself and others, model counterparts, and practical arrangements Which relations are retained and which meanings the author develops further.
Bounded formal translation Represents certain relations through selected symbols, assertions, and rules, and checks their consequences What is represented, what is assumed, and what remains outside the model.

All three levels can belong to the same work, while a reader still needs to know what responsibility a particular sentence carries. For example, the subject Lacan discusses is not a database object; putting certain relations into a formal model makes selected relations inspectable. A derivation within a formal system is also different from having established a reliable personal model through actual conversations.

Five short reading paths are available:

  • To understand “I,” “ego,” and “others,” begin with language and the Other, then read the ego and the divided subject.
  • To understand how a changed participant position can reorganize a problem, read dialectical reversal, then return to the main sequence's how a solution becomes a new problem.
  • To understand why an earlier meaning may only become recognizable later, read retroaction and retrospective understanding, then return to speaking and retrospective meaning.
  • To understand how sustained writing connects with truth, read full speech, half-saying, and truth, then return to half-saying truth and continuing revision.
  • To understand the three registers and the sinthome, begin with the registers, then read the sinthome, and finally return to Forming a sinthome.

Language, signifiers, and the Other

Begin with a relation when approaching the signifier (signifiant): a word, name, or mark works through its differences from and connections to other marks, and through the discourse in which it appears. The description “good student” can connect grades, obedience, expectations, and recognition; in another discourse, the same description may become ironic. Treating it as a label with fixed content misses how it organizes relations between someone and others.

The Other (Autre, often written $A$) names the locus of otherness in which language and discourse find their place. When someone speaks, they already draw on names, distinctions, and expectations they did not create alone. Parents, teachers, institutions, or a current interlocutor may bear these demands and forms of recognition within a particular relationship, but “the Other” is more than a name for any one of them. In his 1966 radio discussion, p. 2, Lacan describes language as the environment in which a person grows up and raises the relation between the unconscious and the discourse of the Other.

Here this adds a question to understanding oneself and others: within what relationship was this sentence spoken, and from what position was it heard? “You can try again” may carry different weight when spoken by a friend, an examiner, or someone with particular significance. Recording the speaker helps recover the event, but understanding their position still requires context. A name or a model-role field alone cannot establish the position of the Other.

A “model counterpart” is also an actual arrangement, with current capabilities, tools, and agreed contributions. Whether a particular model response acquires special authority within this person's relationships is another question to understand. Using a language model does not automatically settle that judgment about the relationship.

The ego and the divided subject

Approach the ego (moi) through how someone recognizes a relatively complete image of themself. Lacan's mirror-stage essay (1949) discusses the subject's identification through an image: the image offers unity while also involving a relation to an external form. “Imaginary” here does not mean “false and therefore useless.” An image can actually organize feelings, expectations, and actions.

The divided subject (sujet barré, often written $\bar S$ or a barred S) concerns the subject's relation to representation by signifiers. In “Subversion of the Subject”, Lacan proposes that a signifier represents the subject for another signifier. The subject acquires a position through these signifying relations, yet cannot be directly equated with the signifier or statement representing them. Division here concerns this constitutive relation, beyond how much information a self-description omits. It cannot be reduced to “a person contradicts themself,” nor is it a popular expression for multiple personalities.

A limited example can make the question recognizable: someone says, “I only want to write the essay well,” while repeatedly asking whether the other person approves of them. Beyond stating a writing goal, what response does this sentence seek from the other person? The statement's content and the relational position from which it is spoken may not fully coincide. The example makes the question visible; interpreting a particular person requires further material. One sentence cannot establish a hidden motive.

This site's personal model is a partial understanding of a person within the current question. A connected self-account, a formal view, and the person who continues expressing and acting therefore need to be understood distinctly. Lacan's distinctions make this non-coincidence worth investigating; they do not directly supply an algorithm for generating personal models.

Metaphor, metonymy, and condensation

In “The Instance of the Letter” (1957), original pagination 505–515, Lacan approaches metaphor and metonymy through relations among signifiers. Metaphor involves one signifier substituting for another in a chain and producing a new effect of meaning; the displaced term remains involved through other connections. Metonymy concerns connections among signifiers and the movement of meaning, beyond the single rhetorical example of a part standing for a whole.

The relations differ. Metaphoric substitution brings a meaning into view: in a fictional account, “the manager became a judge” gives workplace evaluation relations of trial, defense, and verdict. This does not transfer a fixed bundle of every judicial attribute to the manager. Its effect depends on connections to the surrounding discourse. Lacan develops substitution through Hugo's lines about Boaz and his sheaf. Metonymy concerns connections and movement along the chain. In a hypothetical process of desire, expectation might move from publication to a byline to a particular person's recognition. Objects can change while the relation driving the movement remains a question; the succession of three items alone does not establish a mechanism of desire.

In this account, Freud's condensation (Verdichtung) is connected to the superimposition of signifiers and metaphor, while displacement is connected to metonymy. Condensation here belongs to questions about dream-work and the unconscious. It cannot simply be equated with summarization, token reduction, or merging records into a label. This site's relational analogies also draw on other theories; their contributions and differences need explanation through the relations each addresses.

This raises a useful question for personal models: does a compact expression merely shorten material, or has it organized that material anew? “A workshop for joint creation” can gather trial, criticism, and revision while obscuring delegation and completion responsibilities in a particular task. Unfold its relations and return to exchanges that support or challenge them to judge the condensation's fit. Condensing revisable relations develops this site's writing method: a proposal informed by these concepts, not a compression algorithm derived from Lacan.

The subject supposed to know and the position of interpretation

The subject supposed to know (sujet supposé savoir) concerns a position credited with knowledge concerning the subject. In Seminar XI, 10 June 1964, Staferla transcript pp. 161–163, Lacan develops this relation through transference while explaining that the analyst does not thereby possess absolute knowledge. Being supposed to know and actually knowing therefore require separate examination.

This is not another name for knowing a great deal or for trust in general. Within this session's analytic setting, the question concerns whom one addresses and how one expects the other to receive meanings one has not yet grasped. Someone can acknowledge the other's fallibility while still addressing that position of supposed knowledge. The Other as a locus of speech and a person occupying this knowledge position in a particular relationship also cannot simply be equated. The concept questions the relational structure of interpretation rather than ranking people by their quantity of knowledge.

For model collaboration, this raises a question about a personal account's interpretive authority. What comes from sources, actual use, the person's recognition, a sense of completeness, or the model's fluent response? A model interpretation written into an archive and cited by later models acquires no independent support from that repetition. Recognition can show how the account was received without alone establishing its explanation of psychological causes.

This contemporary borrowing examines interpretation, reception, and use; using AI alone does not establish a particular transference relation. A counterpart can contribute understanding the person has not articulated while returning to material, comparing interpretations, and revising accounts it helped form. The account participates in the relationship without acquiring the position of determining the person's final truth.

Dialectical reversal: changing understanding and position

In “Intervention on Transference” (1951), Lacan reads Freud's Dora case through a series of dialectical reversals. Reversal concerns the subject's position within the relations being recounted and what becomes the object of the question, beyond replacing an interpretation with its opposite. Retain the source's particular context of transference and the analytic relationship.

Retroaction and dialectical reversal can therefore connect without being identical. A later sentence can change earlier meaning without establishing a changed subjective position; editing a tool's instructions likewise does not prove such a transformation. The main essay offers a bounded comparison: moving from “receiving help costs independence” to “how can I participate in organizing and changing assistance?” may move the speaker from rejecting assistance toward participating in arranging the relationship. Particular speech and action must support a claim that this change actually occurred.

Hegel's determinate negation and sublation offer an inquiry into determinations and their limits. Science of Logic, “The Absolute Idea,” §§1789–1802 supplies no template for combining arbitrary opposing opinions into a stronger conclusion. At the scale of practice, this site asks what an earlier determination protected, where it begins obstructing its purpose, and how a new relation can retain concerns while changing their form. This comparison and Lacan's question of subjective position have distinct objects; neither makes a software version change automatically a dialectical reversal. Speech, opposition, and self-formation owns the developed contemporary argument.

Retroaction and retrospective understanding

Retroaction (rétroaction) concerns how meaning returns from later connections to earlier expression. A word need not acquire its full meaning at the instant it is spoken; the rest of a sentence, a response, or a later narrative can reorganize how the earlier part is understood. Lacan's “Subversion of the Subject” discusses this return through discourse and relations among signifiers.

For example: “Leaving then cost me a great deal—and it also taught me, for the first time, what I did not want.” The second part places the earlier “cost” within a different relation of meaning. What changes is the present understanding of that departure and its place in the subsequent narrative. A later sentence has not erased the departure that occurred.

“Retrospective understanding” is an interpretive expression in this guide: on later rereading their own expression, receiving a response, or experiencing a new event, someone reinterprets an earlier experience—sometimes recognizing connections previously unclear to them, sometimes forming an understanding they did not previously have. This can be connected to Lacan's retroaction without treating every later understanding as the same Lacanian technical concept. The discussion of the subject's history and the future anterior in “The Function and Field of Speech and Language in Psychoanalysis” (1953), PDF p. 35, original publication p. 144, offers a source route for pursuing this temporal relation. Such later self-understanding can also involve misrecognition and needs continuing examination through material and new encounters.

In this site's writing and model collaboration, the relation can develop as follows: an unfinished expression is retained; the model organizes it into a readable account; the person rereads it, recognizes some connections, and discovers misunderstandings; this recognition changes subsequent expression. A work thus preserves earlier ideas and can also become material for new understanding.

Two questions still need separate treatment: does an interpretation make an experience intelligible, and are its factual judgments about the past warranted? A narrative fitting one's current feelings does not establish that every detail of the past was as it describes. Retaining the original event, original words, and the time an interpretation formed lets retrospective understanding remain constrained by its material. Continue with Forming a life trajectory.

Punctuation and quilting: how meaning becomes provisionally settled

Excerpts from “The Function and Field of Speech and Language” (1953) discuss how punctuation gives discourse meaning, including through the cutting of an analytic session. In “Subversion of the Subject” (1960), Écrits p. 805, the quilting point (point de capiton) concerns the arrest of sliding signification. A sentence's last term retroactively determining its earlier terms provides its diachronic illustration. This is also distinct from Miller's account of “suture.”

For example, an utterance begins “you are right” and continues “the question does need rewriting, but your answer is still unsupported.” The continuation specifies what was endorsed; extracting the opening words would misrepresent the whole position. The quilting point is more than a sentence's final punctuation mark: Lacan also discusses the synchronic organization of meaning. It directs attention to which signifying relations make discourse intelligible, without guaranteeing that this organization exhausts the subject or remains fixed forever.

For our writing, the useful question is when unfolding expression becomes a settled description, and how that punctuation or naming directs later reading. Summarizing “wanting independence” as “rejecting help” installs one interpretation in subsequent collaboration. Continued expression might require “wanting to retain participation in direction and the ability to change delegation.” The new account enables work while remaining open to other tasks and later material.

Compression therefore selects content and can provisionally fix a reading. Sources, applicability conditions, and an unresolved alternative allow that reading to unfold again. This is a proposal for maintaining descriptions; the analogy does not make analytic session-cutting a technique for model dialogue.

Full speech, half-saying, and truth

These concepts raise a further question: how does speech change the subject's relation to their history, and why can that change still not say their whole truth? First distinguish three relations, then follow their source periods.

Relation What it makes visible Consequence for sustained writing
Full speech Speech reorganizes the subject's history and how it is assumed Examine how expression changes someone's relation to their experience.
Retroaction Later signifying connections participate in determining earlier meaning Read a new version as a reinterpretation of earlier expression, beyond counting additions.
The half-saying of truth Truth cannot be exhausted by a complete totality of speech New understanding remains possible, while a present account cannot close subsequent speech.

1953: full speech and the subject's history

Full speech (parole pleine) cannot be measured by the quantity of material. In excerpts from “The Function and Field of Speech and Language in Psychoanalysis”, Lacan connects its effect with reorganizing past contingencies and the meaning of the subject's history as it opens toward a future. Ask how the subject assumes that history in speech addressed to another, beyond acquiring a more complete list of experiences.

A brief statement may change someone's position in understanding their situation; extensive self-description may repeatedly sustain an existing image. This contrast directs attention to what speech does. It supplies no test that classifies speech as full from sentence length, a feeling of candor, or self-identification alone. Connecting writing and model collaboration with this question is this site's extension; its effects require understanding actual exchange and use.

1960: unfolding signifying chains and retroaction

In “Subversion of the Subject”, the temporal relation of meaning receives further construction: a sentence's later parts can retroactively determine how its earlier terms are understood. A signifying chain has an order of unfolding and a relation through which the later acts on the earlier. Connecting it with a personal trajectory requires explaining repetition, substitution, connections, and changes in the positions of words. Timestamped records supply material for that inquiry.

Such development does not guarantee progress in one direction. Later interpretation may open previously unseen connections or force old material into a tidy story. Retaining earlier expression and new responses lets readers compare what actually changed. The preceding section on retroaction and retrospective understanding distinguishes changes in meaning from their factual grounds.

1970–1974: half-saying and the limit of saying all

Half-saying (mi-dire) does not divide truth into two pieces that can be assembled, nor does it mean that a statement is half true and half false. In Seminar XVII, 11 March 1970, transcription p. 47, Lacan uses the enigma as a model for truth's half-saying and distinguishes this form from the division of the subject in the same passage. Related concepts therefore still need their distinctions. In the opening of Television (1974), he connects the impossibility of saying the whole truth with the limits of words and the real. This limit does not arise merely from insufficient present information; more records or revisions cannot be promised to remove it.

This distinguishes several meanings of gradual development. Progressive disclosure in a Skill normally concerns reading existing material as needed. Unfolding speech can also form meanings that did not previously exist. Half-saying concerns the totality such speech cannot complete. These can meet within one practice, but an information-organizing method does not entail Lacan's account of truth. Early full speech and later half-saying cannot be joined into stages of first saying half and eventually saying everything.

Returning to this site, a philosophical Skill can retain present understanding, participate in subsequent collaboration, and undergo revision through new experience and speech. The model's interpretations enter that exchange too; fluency grants them no position of final truth. Examine which relations become possible to articulate, assume, and change; factual judgments still require source checks. The main essay's half-saying truth and continuing revision develops this practice through the independence example. The guide supplies conceptual relations and reading entrances; the main essay develops the site's argument.

The three registers: different relations within the same experience

The Imaginary (Imaginaire) concerns images, a sense of wholeness, and identification; the Symbolic (Symbolique) concerns signifiers, differences, positions, and their organization; the Real (Réel) concerns the impossibility or limits encountered by these organizations of meaning and imagery. They do not sort material into three disjoint boxes. In his later work, Lacan further investigates their connections through knots; excerpts from Seminar XXII, R.S.I., the session of 10 December 1974 offer an entrance.

For example, understanding oneself as an “independent creator” involves an image with which one can identify; the position of “creator” within language, evaluation, and relationships involves symbolic organization; some recurring difficulties may prevent this self-image and explanation from smoothly encompassing experience. The last example is only a way into the question. It does not license calling all unrecorded feelings, unknown data, or bodily responses “the Real.”

This site draws on the registers' emphases to illuminate its practice: philosophy turns toward a real not exhausted by expression; psychology attends to images, identifications, and their organization of experience; engineering makes relations usable through language, rules, and programs. The trinity of philosophy, psychology, and engineering arranges them as resonant analogies: follow a column for its emphasis, cross the columns for their connections. The site's physicalism has its own argument; the Real contributes a question about the limits of expression.

Fantasy and its traversal: the subject's position in a relationship

Fantasy (fantasme) in Lacan concerns the subject's relation to the object of desire and how a scene positions the subject in relation to the Other's desire. It can organize the experience of reality, expected responses, satisfaction, and repetition. Everyday daydreams may supply material; the recurring positions and relations within them matter especially. “The Subversion of the Subject” (1960) locates fantasy among subject, desire, and the Other. Object a in its formula concerns the cause of desire, rather than simply a person or thing one wants.

Suppose someone treats “I have a place with the other only if I continually prove useful” as a necessary condition of relationship. Inquiry concerns both the claim's truth and how the person imagines the other's demands, occupies the position of being judged, and sustains the relation through giving, testing, and anxiety. Actual demands, lived dependencies, and particular experiences remain part of the explanation.

Traversing fantasy concerns a change in the subject's relation to this organization. A seemingly necessary scene and position can become recognizable; their function in sustaining desire and satisfaction can enter analysis, and the subject may cease to depend on them in the same way. Recognizing an inaccurate belief or giving a more complete account of oneself addresses only part of this. The final session of Seminar XI (24 June 1964; Alan Sheridan translation, p. 273) leaves the experience of the drive after traversing the fundamental fantasy as a question. This scholarly concept index retains the source locator. Traversal thus concerns changes in relationship and experience, rather than a checklist of self-explanations to complete.

Its relation to the later sinthome retains two questions: how a subject changes their dependence on a fantasy scene, and how a singular practice sustains their life and jouissance. Scholarship offers different accounts of their connection; see Coffman, 2013. In this site's contemporary use, examining relational position and constructing sustainable arrangements can interweave and revise one another.

The six actual accounts can help organize experiences, articulate questions, and increase self-understanding; concepts can also question the accounts' own premises. Rereading one's patterns: philosophical reflection and loosening fantasy develops this philosophical discussion. It provides no guidance for self-help psychological analysis, assessment, treatment, or traversal of fantasy. Model interpretations and document revisions do not establish psychological mechanisms, clinical traversal, or therapeutic effects.

Sinthome: from Lacan's question to this site's definition

Sinthome is a spelling Lacan adopts in Seminar XXIII. In the particular construction of the 17 February 1976 session, it participates in repairing the knot; in the 11 May session, the relations among Joyce's writing, ego, and the knot are developed further. The question concerns how a particular practice enters this person's mode of existence, beyond what a work expresses through its content.

This site adopts the name with its own concrete referent: a practical arrangement jointly shaped by personal philosophy, psychology, and engineering, including an understanding of the person, the model counterpart they need, and their relationship, together with expressions, tools, and ways of using them. Relevant material informs the arrangement; current technical conditions give it usable form; use brings revision. A Skill can carry some of its understanding and methods, while a harness can organize its actual realization. Life is the setting in which it forms, is used, and has consequences.

Reading “sinthome” here therefore requires recognizing both the term's source and this site's particular definition. The name does not turn all of life into one object or directly make a software package the clinical construction Lacan discusses. How far it helps stabilize life or continue creation needs to be understood through concrete use. See Forming a sinthome for the detailed formation process.

Which relations does formal translation capture?

This site's Speech, opposition, and self-formation uses some formal notation. It gives selected relations an inspectable expression, which readers can consider alongside the concepts above.

Relation of interest Expression used here Scope of the expression
What someone said and within which relationship A speech record containing speaker, situation, time, and address Retains available event content; subsequent interpretation still needs grounds.
What a selected self-account entails Conceptual constraints, selected assertions, and their formal consequences Checks inferences within the given representation without exhausting ego or subject.
How later understanding returns to earlier expression Relations among earlier expression, present context, and the time of interpretation Locates changes in interpretation without using one symbol to explain every mechanism of retroaction.
How a personal model enters actual collaboration Counterpart models, expression, Skills, tools, and relations of use Forms a concrete arrangement whose adequacy still needs examination against the person's material and actual results.

Formalization and personal understanding can help each other: clear representation can expose omissions, while new material may force the representation to change. Translating relations into a language, forming an interpretation from material, and computing under given assumptions are connected but different activities. This also explains why a theoretical conceptual model, an event archive covering partial situations, and temporary models formed for the current question can coexist.

From formalization to human–machine interaction: exploratory contributions

Formalization can make an interpretation's choices inspectable: which objects are represented, which relations become rules, and what those rules produce. The studies below offer different constructions and questions. Together they do not establish a validated personal-model method. This account selects their specific contributions while distinguishing the authors' proposals from its own extensions.

From relations to computation. Li and Li (2025) represent RSI as message-passing active-inference units and investigate synchronization and collective dynamics through dyadic and triadic simulations. They acknowledge the construction's abstraction and incomplete treatment of fantasy's axiomatic function, complex topology, and desire's diachronic metonymy. This encourages an explicit account of what a translation preserves. Coupled trajectories alone establish neither Borromean topology nor an actual person's mechanism of desire. Santos and Dunker's study of fantasy uses paraconsistent logic to propose that fantasy renders the signifying chain consistent. Retaining unresolved differences deserves investigation; that does not identify every conflict as fantasy or a change of logic as clinical change. The article belongs to issue 41 (2021), published online in 2023.

From machines to interaction. Possati (2020) brings Lacan and Latour to cycles of human identification, machine response, and renewed interpretation, proposing an “algorithmic unconscious” research direction. Li and Li's FreeAgent preprint (2024) places ChatGPT in an interpreting role within a demonstration connecting bodily images and symbolic identification. The former is a philosophical interpretation, the latter a simplified construction. They raise questions about technical mediation of self-understanding without establishing human unconscious processes or self-awareness in machines. How an actual response is received remains a question about the particular interaction.

Distinguishing explanatory scales. Li et al.'s Perspective (2026) distinguishes mechanistic, behavioral, and interactive accounts of models and examines what metaphors reveal and obscure. This supports separate examination of implementation, observed activity, and position within collaboration. This site adopts that distinction of questions without treating the proposed “machine experientialism” as comprehensively validated or inferring internal mechanisms directly from relational positions.

Distinguishing memory from generated state. Shen et al.'s TSJ preprint (2026), §7.7, separates observable interaction memories from separately generated psychological states and retrieves memories for later scenarios. Section 7.13 also separates judging from trajectory generation. This is an engineering reference for distinguishing events, interpretations, and consequences. Its personas, state updates, and scores serve simulation-based evaluation rather than measurements of actual people. Retrospectively selecting an earlier event does not itself establish causation. This site retains those distinctions without copying the psychological scores or state equations.

Return to the sources, then to this site

The table lists entrances in chronological order. It helps locate a concept without requiring a first-time reader to complete every text in sequence.

Source entrance Questions to pursue Return to this site
1949: The mirror stage How does an image participate in identification, and why can the ego not simply be treated as a transparent inner fact? Self-description and formal views
1951: Intervention on Transference How does dialectical reversal concern the subject's position in the relations recounted? Dialectical reversal
1953: The function and field of speech and language How does full speech reorganize the past, and how does the subject assume their history? Full speech and the subject's history
1960: Subversion of the Subject How do subject, Other, signifier, and retroaction connect? The Other and retrospective meaning
1966: Radio discussion, p. 2 What does growing up within language mean for the subject? Personal understanding
1969: Seminar XVII, 26 November How does a position in discourse differ from its actual speaker? Signifying chains and works
1970: Seminar XVII, 11 March, p. 47 How does the enigma illuminate half-saying, and how does it differ from subjective division? Half-saying and the limit of saying all
1974: Television, opening Why does continuing speech not amount to eventually saying the whole truth? Half-saying truth and continuing revision
1974–1975: R.S.I. excerpts Why do connections among the registers become a question, and how do knots enter the discussion? The general Trinity and its individual instance
1976: Sinthome, 17 February; 11 May How do particular writing and practices participate in a person's knot? Forming a sinthome

This timeline points to conceptual development: mirror identification, language and the subject, and the later knot discussions each have their own questions and contexts. Later terms can help reread earlier questions without implying that the earlier texts already contained the entire later theory. On returning to this site, retain a simple reading movement: identify what question the original concept answers, see which relation this account selects, then check whether that relation remains clear in expression and realization.
